questions.q: Besides a plain string, what other content shapes can a tool_result block actually carry, per the Claude API?
options: Only XML documents, nothing else
Only base64-encoded binary data
Text block(s), an image, a document block, or no content at all for a side-effect-only tool
Tool results can never carry anything other than a plain string
questions.explain: The real API accepts text blocks, images, document blocks, or an empty result — not just a bare string, as Lesson 3's simplest example showed.

questions.q: Why is passing a full raw weather API response (coordinates, pressure, wind, numeric codes, etc.) back as a tool_result usually a bad idea?
options: It's actually the ideal format and should always be passed through unmodified
It wastes context on fields the model doesn't need and forces it to dig the relevant value out of a nested structure
The Claude API technically rejects any JSON object as tool_result content
Raw API responses are always smaller than formatted summaries
questions.explain: A bloated payload buries the one or two values that actually matter; formatting it down to something like '91°F, clear' is the same high-signal principle Lesson 6 applied to schema design, now applied to every actual result.

questions.q: What does this lesson say about treating tool_result content sourced from outside your control (a web page, an email, a third-party API)?
options: It should be treated as untrusted, since an attacker who can influence it could embed hidden instructions trying to redirect Claude
It should always be inserted directly into the system prompt for maximum authority
It can be safely ignored, since tools never return anything risky
It should be converted to plain English and told to the user verbatim, with no review
questions.explain: This is Anthropic's own guidance: keep untrusted content inside proper tool_result blocks rather than a system prompt or plain text block, where it could carry more apparent authority than it should — directly relevant to Chapter 5's lesson on prompt injection.

questions.q: Is an empty tool_result (just a tool_use_id, with no content field) considered valid?
options: No, every tool_result must always include non-empty content
No, an empty tool_result always triggers an automatic retry
Yes, but only for the very first tool call in a conversation
Yes — it's valid and useful for a side-effect tool, like marking something as read, that has nothing further to report
questions.explain: A tool_result's content field is optional; a tool whose entire purpose is a side effect, not a return value, can validly send back no content at all.

questions.q: What principle connects Lesson 6's schema design guidance to this lesson's advice on formatting tool output?
options: There's no connection between the two lessons at all
The high-signal principle — returning only what the model needs — applies both when designing a tool's response shape and every time an actual call produces a real payload
Lesson 6 only applies to input parameters, never to anything related to output
Formatting tool output is unrelated to schema design in every respect
questions.explain: Lesson 6 introduced high-signal output as a schema-design idea; this lesson applies that same discipline live, to the actual bloated payload a real tool call returns, not just its documented shape.
